claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5 wt% yttrium to a high-entropy-alloy bond coat will improve coating durability and reliability.
High-entropy-alloy bond coats without reactive-element doping typically exhibit limited oxidation-scale adhesion.
At 1100–1200 °C in air, protective oxide scales on these bond coats are challenged by spallation.
At 1100–1200 °C in air, these bond coats undergo microstructural degradation.
Yttrium segregates at the alloy/oxide interface during high-temperature exposure.
Interfacial yttrium promotes formation of a denser and more adherent oxide scale.
The yttrium-promoted oxide scale is likely alumina.
Yttrium addition reduces oxide-scale porosity and void formation at the alloy/oxide interface.
Yttrium stabilizes the oxide microstructure during cyclic oxidation.
Mitigation of interfacial voids and stabilization of the oxide microstructure enhance thermally grown oxide adhesion and integrity.
Improved oxide adhesion and integrity reduce spallation and extend the bond coat's functional life.
The yttrium-doped bond coat will increase time to spallation and lifetime by approximately 20–50% relative to an undoped bond coat under high-temperature thermal cycling.
The beneficial effect is expected only under oxidizing conditions at 1100–1200 °C.
The beneficial effect might not extend to reducing environments.
Reactive-element addition could induce phase instabilities under some conditions.
